--- title: "17 · Model-Free Methods" subtitle: "Part III — Model Uncertainty" jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Executed in:** Python · **Book:** ADM Ch. 17 · **Lecture:** to be added ::: ## Big picture ### Where this chapter fits [Chapter 16](ch16-model-based-methods.qmd) learned a model of the world and planned on it. That works well when the state space is small enough to count transitions in. **Model-free** methods skip the model entirely: they learn the action value function $Q(s, a)$, how good each action is in each state, straight from experience. There's no transition table to fill in and no planning step, just a small correction to $Q$ after every step. This is the core of practical reinforcement learning, from classic Q-learning to the deep Q-networks that learned to play Atari games. [Chapter 18](ch18-imitation-learning.qmd) turns to learning from an expert's demonstrations instead of from rewards. **The question:** how can an agent learn good action values from its own experience, one step at a time, without ever writing down the dynamics? The short answer: **nudge each estimate toward a one-step target.** An average can be learned incrementally: move the estimate a fraction $\alpha$ of the way toward each new sample. **Q-learning** uses the sample $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$, the reward plus the best value available next, and learns the *optimal* action values even while exploring. **Sarsa** uses the action actually taken next, and learns the values of the policy it follows, exploration included. **Eligibility traces** pass each update back along the recent path, so a distant reward is learned quickly. **Reward shaping** adds hints, safely if they take a potential-based form. With **function approximation**, the same updates become gradient steps on parameters, and **experience replay** reuses past experience to make them efficient and stable. ```{dot} //| label: fig-ch17-map //| fig-width: 6.8 //| fig-height: 3.7 //| fig-cap: "Map of this chapter. One idea, incremental estimation toward a sampled target, gives Q-learning and Sarsa; the rest speed them up or scale them up." //| fig-alt: "Diagram. A blue box, Incremental mean (step toward each sample), points to two boxes: Q-learning (target uses the best next action; off-policy) and Sarsa (target uses the next action taken; on-policy). Sarsa points to Eligibility traces (pass credit back along the path). Both Q-learning and Sarsa point to Reward shaping (hints that keep the optimum: potential-based). Q-learning points to Function approximation (gradient Q-learning), which points to Experience replay (reuse past tuples)." digraph ch17 { rankdir=TB; bgcolor="#fcfcfb"; pad=0.25; nodesep=0.35; ranksep=0.45; node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="white", color="#c3c2b7", penwidth=1.2, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13, fontcolor="#0b0b0b", margin="0.12,0.07"]; edge [color="#52514e", penwidth=1.2, arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, fontcolor="#52514e"]; inc [label=<Incremental mean
step toward each sample>, fillcolor="#cde2fb", color="#2a78d6"]; q [label=<Q-learning
best next action; off-policy>]; sarsa [label=<Sarsa
next action taken; on-policy>]; traces [label=<Eligibility traces
credit flows back>]; shaping [label=<Reward shaping
potential-based hints>]; approx [label=<Function approximation
gradient Q-learning>]; replay [label=<Experience replay
reuse past tuples>]; inc -> q [label="target: max"]; inc -> sarsa [label="target: a′"]; sarsa -> traces; q -> shaping; sarsa -> shaping; q -> approx [label="scale up"]; approx -> replay; } ``` ### The key ideas at a glance 1. **Incremental estimation.** To learn an average from a stream of samples, keep an estimate and move it a fraction $\alpha$ of the way toward each new sample. With $\alpha = 1/m$ it is exactly the running average. With a constant $\alpha$ it tracks recent samples and never quite settles. The gap between the sample and the estimate is a **temporal difference error**. 2. **Q-learning.** The value of taking $a$ in $s$ is, on average, the reward plus the discounted value of the best action from wherever you land. Each experience $(s, a, r, s')$ gives one sample of that, $r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')$; move $Q(s, a)$ toward it. Q-learning is **off-policy**: it learns the values of the greedy policy while behaving differently, for example exploring with ε-greedy. 3. **Sarsa.** Use the action $a'$ actually taken next instead of the best one: the target is $r + \gamma Q(s', a')$. Sarsa is **on-policy**: it learns the values of the policy it follows, exploration included. Near a cliff, that makes it cautious, because it knows it sometimes stumbles. 4. **Eligibility traces.** One-step updates pass news of a reward back only one state per visit. Traces keep a fading memory of recently visited state-action pairs, and apply each update to all of them in proportion. A reward found at the end of a long path is credited to the whole path at once. 5. **Reward shaping.** Sparse rewards make learning slow; adding intermediate rewards can speed it up, but can also change what is optimal. Shaping of the form $F = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)$, a difference of **potentials**, never changes the optimal policy. 6. **Function approximation and experience replay.** With too many states for a table, represent $Q_\theta(s, a)$ with parameters and turn the update into a gradient step. **Experience replay** stores recent experience and learns from random batches of it, which reuses data and breaks up the correlations between consecutive steps. ### Vocabulary | Term | Plain meaning | |:---|:---| | Model-free learning | Learning values or policies directly, without estimating $T$ and $R$ | | Learning rate $\alpha$ | How far each update moves an estimate toward its new sample | | Temporal difference (TD) error | Sampled target minus current estimate | | Q-learning | TD learning of $Q$ with target $r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ | | Sarsa | TD learning of $Q$ with target $r + \gamma Q(s', a')$, using the next action taken | | On-policy / off-policy | Learning the values of the policy being followed / of a different policy | | Eligibility trace $N(s, a)$ | A decaying record of how recently and often a pair was visited | | Reward shaping $F(s, a, s')$ | Extra reward added during training to guide learning | | Potential function $\beta(s)$ | A score of states whose differences define safe shaping | | Experience replay | Storing past transitions and learning from random batches of them | : Terms used on this page. {#tbl-vocab} ### After this chapter you can - Estimate a mean incrementally, and choose a learning rate schedule. - Implement Q-learning and Sarsa, and explain when they learn different policies. - Speed up learning with eligibility traces, optimistic initialization, and potential-based reward shaping, and recognize shaping that changes the optimal policy. - Apply Q-learning with linear function approximation, and use experience replay. ## Intuition ::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"} You're learning how long each route to work takes, without a map. - **Incremental averaging:** every trip, you adjust your estimate for the route you took a little toward that day's time. - **Q-learning:** you judge the first leg of a trip by the time it took *plus the best time you know* from where it left you, even if today you took a detour from there. - **Sarsa:** you judge it by what you *actually did* next, detours included. If you often take detours, Sarsa's estimates include them. - **Traces:** when a trip turns out great, you credit the whole route, not just the last turn. - **Shaping:** a friend's hint ("the closer to the river, the faster") helps you learn, as long as it can't lure you into driving in circles. ::: ### Moving averages Bus waits average 8 minutes but vary a lot. With $\alpha = 1/m$ the estimate is the exact running average; after 300 waits its typical error is 0\.46 minutes. A constant $\alpha = 0.3$ keeps chasing the latest waits, with an error of 3\.3 minutes that never shrinks. A schedule that decays too fast, $\alpha = 1/m^{1.5}$, stops learning before it has enough data: error 2\.1 (@fig-incremental). See @eq-incremental. ### One step of truth, then trust your estimates Q-learning never sees the rules of Hex World. It moves each $Q(s, a)$ toward the reward just received plus the best $Q$ at the next tile. After 1\,432 steps of ε-greedy experience, its greedy policy is worth 3\.16 on average; after 30\,000, 4\.29 (the optimum is 4\.53). See @eq-q-learning. ### Learning the policy you follow On a towpath beside a canal, the shortest route runs right along the edge. Q-learning learns that route (9 steps), because it values the *best* next move. But while it still explores 10% of the time, it keeps stumbling into the water: it averaged \-31\.1 per episode late in training. Sarsa learns the value of its own stumbling policy, so it prefers a path that stays at least 2 rows from the water, 13 steps long, and averaged \-20\.6 (@fig-towpath). See @eq-sarsa. ### Pass the credit back When Sarsa reaches a reward, only the last step's value changes. Eligibility traces also update the steps before it, fading with distance. On Hex World, after 1\,432 steps, Sarsa's greedy policy was worth 3\.48, and Sarsa(λ) with λ = 0.5 3\.78 (@fig-hex-learning). See @eq-traces. ### Hints that don't mislead On the mountain trail of Chapter 16, Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration learned to climb in 0% of 20 runs. Adding a potential-based hint, "being higher is worth 1 per position", it learned in 85%. A naive hint, "+5 for every step up", backfires: the policy that is optimal for the hinted rewards walks down from the summit so it can earn the bonus again, and never enjoys the view. See @eq-shaping. ### Scale up with parameters, reuse with replay For the mountain car, a table won't do: position and speed are continuous. Q-learning with a linear function of 49 Fourier features needed 178 steps per episode after 100 episodes. Replaying random batches of stored experience, it needed 123 (@fig-mountain-car). See @eq-gradient-q and @eq-replay. ## Formalism ### Incremental estimation of the mean The average of $m$ samples can be updated one sample at a time (ADM §17.1): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Incremental mean"} $$ \hat x_m = \hat x_{m-1} + \alpha(m)\big(x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}\big), \qquad \sum_{m=1}^\infty \alpha(m) = \infty,\quad \sum_{m=1}^\infty \alpha(m)^2 < \infty $$ {#eq-incremental} ::: **In words.** Move the estimate a fraction of the way toward each new sample. For the estimate to converge, the steps must shrink, but not too fast. **Term by term.** - $x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}$ is the **temporal difference error**: how much the new sample surprised the old estimate. - With $\alpha(m) = 1/m$, $\hat x_m$ is exactly the sample mean. - The first condition keeps the steps large enough to reach the answer from any start. The second keeps them small enough for the noise to average out. $1/m$ and $1/m^{0.6}$ satisfy both. $1/m^{1.5}$ fails the first: its steps shrink so fast that the estimate stops early. A constant $\alpha$ fails the second: it keeps fluctuating, but it tracks a mean that drifts. - With a constant $\alpha$, the estimate is a weighted average in which a sample $k$ updates old has weight $\alpha(1 - \alpha)^k$: an exponential moving average. **Why it holds.** $\hat x_m = \frac1m \sum_{i \le m} x^{(i)} = \frac1m\big(x^{(m)} + (m - 1)\hat x_{m-1}\big) = \hat x_{m-1} + \frac1m\big(x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}\big)$. The conditions on $\alpha$ are the Robbins–Monro conditions for stochastic approximation (H. Robbins and S. Monro, *Annals of Mathematical Statistics*, 1951). ### Q-learning The action value satisfies the Bellman equation $Q(s, a) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \max_{a'} Q(s', a')$, which is an expectation over the next state. Replace the expectation with one sample, and use the incremental update (ADM §17.2; C. J. C. H. Watkins, 1989): ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Q-learning"} $$ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Big) $$ {#eq-q-learning} ::: **In words.** After each step, move the value of what you just did toward what you got plus the best you believe you can do from where you landed. **Term by term.** - $r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ is the target: a one-sample estimate of the right side of the Bellman optimality equation, using the current $Q$ for the future. - The target doesn't depend on which action the agent takes next, so the agent may explore freely while learning the greedy policy's values. That is what **off-policy** means. - The max over noisy estimates tends to overestimate, a bias that **double Q-learning** reduces. - If every pair is tried infinitely often and $\alpha$ meets the conditions of @eq-incremental for each pair, $Q$ converges to $Q^*$. **Why it holds.** In expectation over $(r, s')$ the target equals the Bellman backup of $Q$, and that backup is a contraction (Chapter 7). So Q-learning is a noisy, sample-by-sample version of value iteration on $Q$, and stochastic approximation theory handles the noise. ### Sarsa Sarsa uses the quintuple $(s, a, r, s', a')$, where $a'$ is the action the agent actually takes next (ADM §17.3; G. A. Rummery and M. Niranjan, 1994): ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Sarsa"} $$ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma\, Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Big) $$ {#eq-sarsa} ::: **In words.** Move the value of what you did toward what you got plus the value of what you actually do next. **Term by term.** - The target uses $Q(s', a')$ for the action chosen by the behavior policy (for example ε-greedy), not the maximum. - So Sarsa estimates $Q^\pi$ for the policy $\pi$ it follows, exploration included: it is **on-policy**. - If exploration is reduced over time, so that the policy becomes greedy in the limit, Sarsa too converges to $Q^*$. **Why it holds.** In expectation, the target is the Bellman *expectation* backup for the behavior policy, $R + \gamma \sum_{s'} T \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s') Q(s', a')$. Sarsa is a sampled version of policy evaluation for the policy it follows, and it improves as that policy improves. ### Eligibility traces Keep a trace $N(s, a)$ for every pair. With the Sarsa TD error $\delta = r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)$, each step does (ADM §17.4): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Sarsa(λ) with eligibility traces"} $$ N(s, a) \leftarrow N(s, a) + 1; \qquad Q(\tilde s, \tilde a) \leftarrow Q(\tilde s, \tilde a) + \alpha\,\delta\, N(\tilde s, \tilde a)\ \ \text{and}\ \ N(\tilde s, \tilde a) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda N(\tilde s, \tilde a)\ \ \text{for all } (\tilde s, \tilde a) $$ {#eq-traces} ::: **In words.** Every pair visited recently gets a share of the current surprise, a smaller share the longer ago it was visited. **Term by term.** - $N(\tilde s, \tilde a)$ counts visits, decaying by $\gamma\lambda$ per step: a pair visited $k$ steps ago has trace $(\gamma\lambda)^k$ (if visited once). - $\lambda = 0$ is plain Sarsa. $\lambda \to 1$ credits the whole episode, like a Monte Carlo return. - Traces are reset at the start of each episode. - With Q-learning, traces must be cut whenever an exploratory action is taken, or they credit the greedy policy with the explorer's outcomes (Watkins's $Q(\lambda)$). **Why it holds.** Summing the trace-weighted updates over an episode gives approximately the update toward a **λ-return**, an average of $n$-step returns with weights $(1 - \lambda)\lambda^{n-1}$. It is the same blend of short and long lookaheads as generalized advantage estimation in Chapter 13 (R. S. Sutton, *Machine Learning*, 1988). ### Reward shaping During training, add $F(s, a, s')$ to the reward. In general this changes the optimal policy, but not if $F$ is a difference of potentials (ADM §17.5; A. Y. Ng, D. Harada and S. Russell, *ICML*, 1999): ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Potential-based reward shaping"} $$ F(s, a, s') = \gamma\, \beta(s') - \beta(s) $$ {#eq-shaping} ::: **In words.** Reward progress in a "potential" score, discounting the new state's score as the future is discounted. **Term by term.** - $\beta(s)$ is any function of the state, for example minus the distance to a goal. On the trail we use $\beta(s) = s$, the position. - Along any trajectory, the shaping terms telescope: $\sum_t \gamma^t F_t = \gamma^T\beta(s_T) - \beta(s_0)$. So every policy's value shifts by $-\beta(s_0)$ (plus a vanishing term), which is the same for every policy starting from $s_0$. - A bonus that isn't of this form, like "+5 for every step up", can be collected in loops, creating new optima that the designer never intended. **Why it holds.** With shaping, the optimal action values become $Q'^*(s, a) = Q^*(s, a) - \beta(s)$. Subtracting a function of the state alone doesn't change which action is best. Ng, Harada and Russell also showed the converse: shaping that preserves the optimal policy for every MDP must have this form. ### Action value function approximation With a parameterized $Q_\theta$, minimize $\frac12\mathbb{E}[(Q^*(s, a) - Q_\theta(s, a))^2]$ by stochastic gradient descent, replacing the unknown $Q^*(s, a)$ by the one-step target (ADM §17.6): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Gradient Q-learning"} $$ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a)\Big)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s, a) $$ {#eq-gradient-q} ::: **In words.** Move the parameters so that $Q_\theta(s, a)$ comes closer to the target, in proportion to the TD error. **Term by term.** - For a linear $Q_\theta(s, a) = \theta_a^\top \phi(s)$, the gradient is the feature vector $\phi(s)$ in the block of $\theta$ for action $a$. - The target also depends on $\theta$, but the update treats it as fixed: a "semi-gradient". That is one reason such methods can diverge. Scaling each step to a bounded norm (Chapter 12), as here, helps. - Every update changes $Q_\theta$ everywhere the features overlap, which generalizes across states, but can also overwrite what was learned elsewhere ("catastrophic forgetting"). **Why it holds.** With the true $Q^*$ in place of the target, it is exactly stochastic gradient descent on the squared error: the gradient of $\frac12(Q^* - Q_\theta)^2$ is $-(Q^* - Q_\theta)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta$. The one-step target is Q-learning's estimate of $Q^*$. ### Experience replay Store the most recent transitions in a buffer. Periodically sample a random batch of $m_{\text{grad}}$ of them and step along their average gradient (ADM §17.7; L.-J. Lin, 1992; V. Mnih et al., 2013): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Replayed gradient Q-learning"} $$ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \frac{\alpha}{m_{\text{grad}}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{\text{grad}}}\Big(r^{(i)} + \gamma\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s'^{(i)}, a') - Q_\theta(s^{(i)}, a^{(i)})\Big)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s^{(i)}, a^{(i)}) $$ {#eq-replay} ::: **In words.** Learn from a random handful of past experiences at once, not just the latest one. **Term by term.** - Each tuple $(s^{(i)}, a^{(i)}, r^{(i)}, s'^{(i)})$ comes from the buffer, which holds recent experience from older versions of the policy. Because Q-learning is off-policy, that's fine. - Averaging over a batch reduces the variance of the step, and sampling at random breaks the correlation between consecutive steps. - Each experience is used many times, which improves data efficiency. - In this page's code the step is taken every step (the book takes one every $m$ steps, discarding the $m$ oldest tuples), and scaled to norm at most 1. **Why it holds.** It is minibatch stochastic gradient descent on the same objective as @eq-gradient-q. The data are drawn from the recent experience distribution instead of the current state alone. ## Worked example ### A running average by hand Four bus waits: 12, 6, 9 and 3 minutes, starting from $\hat x_0 = 0$. | Wait $m$ | Sample | $\alpha = 1/m$: $\hat x_m$ | $\alpha = 0.5$: $\hat x_m$ | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | 12 | $0 + 1 \times 12 = 12$ | $0 + 0.5 \times 12 = 6$ | | 2 | 6 | $12 + \tfrac12(6 - 12) = 9$ | $6 + 0.5(6 - 6) = 6$ | | 3 | 9 | $9 + \tfrac13(9 - 9) = 9$ | $6 + 0.5(9 - 6) = 7.5$ | | 4 | 3 | $9 + \tfrac14(3 - 9) = 7.5$ | $7.5 + 0.5(3 - 7.5) = 5.25$ | : Incremental estimates of the mean wait. {#tbl-incremental} With $\alpha = 1/m$, the last estimate is the exact average, $30/4 = 7.5$. With $\alpha = 0.5$, the most recent wait counts half, and the first one only $0.5^4 = 1/16$. Starting from 0 also drags that estimate down. ### Q-learning and Sarsa disagree by the canal On the towpath, the agent walks east along the row right next to the canal (reward −1 per step, $\gamma = 1$, $\alpha = 0.5$). Suppose its current estimates at the new cell are: $Q(\text{east}) = -8$, the best, along the edge; $Q(\text{north}) = -10$; $Q(\text{south}) = -101$, into the canal. It currently estimates $Q(\text{east})$ at its old cell as $-10$. - **Q-learning** uses the best next value: target $-1 + (-8) = -9$, so $Q \leftarrow -10 + 0.5(-9 - (-10)) = -9.5$. - **Sarsa** uses the action actually taken next. If ε-greedy happened to pick "south" (probability $0.1 / 4 = 0.025$), the target is $-1 + (-101) = -102$, and $Q \leftarrow -10 + 0.5(-102 + 10) = -56$. Sarsa's value of standing by the water absorbs the occasional stumble; Q-learning's doesn't. Averaged over many visits, Sarsa learns that edge cells are worth less *for an agent that explores*. So it routes further from the water, where a stumble costs only a step. ### A trace in three steps Sarsa(λ) with $\gamma = 0.9$, $\lambda = 0.8$, so traces decay by 0.72 per step. The agent visits $(s_1, a_1)$, then $(s_2, a_2)$, then $(s_3, a_3)$, and at the third step receives a surprise $\delta = 5$. The traces are then $0.72^2 = 0.518$, $0.72$ and $1$. With $\alpha = 0.1$ the three values change by $0.1 \times 5 \times (0.518, 0.72, 1) = (0.26, 0.36, 0.5)$. Plain Sarsa would change only the last, by 0.5. ## Interactive ### Q-learning versus Sarsa on the towpath Scrub through training. Each cell shows its current greedy action, and is shaded by its estimated value (darker is worse). The blue line is the greedy path from start (S) to finish (F); the bottom row between them is the canal. ```{ojs} towData = FileAttachment("data/ch17-towpath.json").json() viewof towEp = Inputs.range([5, 500], {step: 5, value: 50, label: "Episodes"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| label: fig-towpath-explorer //| fig-cap: "Greedy actions and values on the towpath after the chosen number of training episodes (one run each; α = 0.5, ε = 0.1). Left: Q-learning. Right: Sarsa. The blue line is the greedy path; the light blue cells are the canal." //| fig-alt: "Interactive pair of 4 by 8 grids. The bottom row between the start (S, bottom left) and the finish (F, bottom right) is shaded light blue as the canal. Each other cell shows an arrow for its greedy action and a grey shade for its value. A blue line traces the greedy path. As the slider increases, Q-learning's path settles along the row right above the canal, while Sarsa's path settles on a row further from the water." { const S = 44, pad = 10, arrow = ["↑", "→", "↓", "←"]; const panel = name => { const snap = towData.snaps[name][towEp / towData.every - 1]; // Follow the greedy actions from the start (at most 40 moves) to draw the path. const move = [[-1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [0, -1]]; let r = towData.rows - 1, c = 0, path = [[r, c]]; for (let k = 0; k < 40 && !(r === towData.rows - 1 && c === towData.cols - 1); k++) { const a = snap.best[r * towData.cols + c]; let r2 = Math.min(Math.max(r + move[a][0], 0), towData.rows - 1), c2 = Math.min(Math.max(c + move[a][1], 0), towData.cols - 1); if (r2 === towData.rows - 1 && c2 > 0 && c2 < towData.cols - 1) { r2 = towData.rows - 1; c2 = 0; } // into the canal r = r2; c = c2; path.push([r, c]); } const shade = d3.scaleLinear([-30, 0], ["#9a9890", "#ffffff"]).clamp(true); const cells = d3.range(towData.rows * towData.cols).map(i => { const r = Math.floor(i / towData.cols), c = i % towData.cols; const canal = r === towData.rows - 1 && c > 0 && c < towData.cols - 1; const label = i === towData.start ? "S" : i === towData.goal ? "F" : canal ? `; } ``` ### Learning rates, live Draw a stream of bus waits (average 8 minutes) and compare a constant learning rate with a decaying one, $\alpha = 1/m^p$. ```{ojs} viewof alphaConst = Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {step: 0.01, value: 0.1, label: "Constant α"}) viewof decayP = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {step: 0.05, value: 1, label: "Decay exponent p"}) viewof waitSeed = Inputs.range([1, 50], {step: 1, value: 1, label: "Random stream"}) ``` ```{ojs} waitRun = { // Exponential waits with mean 8 from a seeded generator; running estimates from 0. const rand = d3.randomExponential.source(d3.randomLcg(waitSeed / 51))(1 / 8); let c = 0, d = 0; return d3.range(1, 201).map(m => { const x = rand(); c += alphaConst * (x - c); d += Math.pow(m, -decayP) * (x - d); return {m, x, constant: c, decaying: d}; }); } md`After 200 waits: constant α gives **${waitRun[199].constant.toFixed(2)}**, decaying α gives **${waitRun[199].decaying.toFixed(2)}** (true mean 8).` ``` ```{ojs} //| label: fig-alpha-explorer //| fig-cap: "Incremental estimates of the mean wait from one random stream of 200 waits: constant α (orange) and α = 1/m^p (blue), with the individual waits as grey dots and the true mean dotted." //| fig-alt: "Interactive chart with wait number 1 to 200 across and minutes up the side, showing grey dots for individual waits scattered from 0 to about 40, a dotted line at 8, an orange line for the constant learning rate and a blue line for the decaying one. A large constant alpha makes the orange line jump with each wait; a small one makes it rise slowly from 0. A decay exponent near 1 makes the blue line settle near 8; a large exponent freezes it early." Plot.plot({ width: 600, height: 300, style: {background: "#fcfcfb"}, x: {label: "wait number m"}, y: {label: "minutes", domain: [0, 25], grid: true}, marks: [ Plot.dot(waitRun, {x: "m", y: "x", r: 1.5, fill: "#898781", fillOpacity: 0.5, clip: true}), Plot.ruleY([8], {strokeDasharray: "3,3"}), Plot.line(waitRun, {x: "m", y: "constant", stroke: "#eb6834", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.line(waitRun, {x: "m", y: "decaying", stroke: "#2a78d6", strokeWidth: 2}) ] }) ``` ## Algorithms & code ### Tabular learners ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def incremental_mean(xs, alpha): """Running estimates x_hat_m = x_hat_{m-1} + alpha(m) (x_m - x_hat_{m-1}) (eq. 17.5), starting from 0. alpha(m) = 1/m gives the sample mean.""" est, out = 0.0, [] for m, x in enumerate(xs, start=1): est += alpha(m) * (x - est) out.append(est) return np.array(out) def epsilon_greedy(q, epsilon, rng): """A random action w.p. epsilon, else a greedy one (ties at random).""" if rng.random() < epsilon: return int(rng.integers(len(q))) return int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(q == q.max()))) class QLearning: """Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha (r + gamma max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)) (eq. 17.10): off-policy, it learns the greedy policy's values while following an exploring one.""" def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, q0=0.0): self.Q = np.full((n_states, n_actions), float(q0)) self.gamma, self.alpha = gamma, alpha def start(self): """Called at the start of each episode (nothing to reset here).""" def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2): target = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2].max() self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * (target - self.Q[s, a]) class Sarsa(QLearning): """Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha (r + gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)) (eq. 17.11), with a' the action actually taken next: on-policy, it learns the values of the exploring policy itself.""" def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2): target = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2, a2] self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * (target - self.Q[s, a]) class SarsaLambda(QLearning): """Sarsa with eligibility traces (eqs. 17.12-17.14). N[s, a] is a decaying visit count; each TD error delta updates every pair in proportion to it, so reward flows back along the recent path.""" def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, lam, q0=0.0): super().__init__(n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, q0) self.lam = lam self.N = np.zeros_like(self.Q) def start(self): self.N[:] = 0.0 # traces don't cross episodes def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2): self.N[s, a] += 1 delta = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2, a2] - self.Q[s, a] self.Q += self.alpha * delta * self.N # every pair, by its trace self.N *= self.gamma * self.lam def run_tabular(env, learner, steps, s0, rng, epsilon=0.1, reset=None, shaping=None, on_step=None): """Learn on a DiscreteMDP env for `steps` steps with epsilon-greedy actions on learner.Q. reset(s2, rng) returns a new start state when an episode ends (and None otherwise). shaping(s, s2) is added to the reward the learner sees (not to the reward recorded). on_step(t, learner) is called after every step. Returns the rewards received. """ n_s = env.R.shape[0] rewards = np.zeros(steps) s = s0 learner.start() a = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s], epsilon, rng) for t in range(steps): s2 = rng.choice(n_s, p=env.T[s, a]) r = env.R[s, a] a2 = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s2], epsilon, rng) # Sarsa needs a' bonus = 0.0 if shaping is None else shaping(s, s2) learner.update(s, a, r + bonus, s2, a2) rewards[t] = r s, a = s2, a2 start = None if reset is None else reset(s, rng) if start is not None: # new episode s = start learner.start() a = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s], epsilon, rng) if on_step is not None: on_step(t, learner) return rewards def potential_shaping(beta, gamma): """F(s, s') = gamma beta(s') - beta(s) (eq. 17.15): shaping that provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged.""" return lambda s, s2: gamma * beta[s2] - beta[s] ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra import Distributions hw = hex_world() # states 1..27; the last one is the terminal nS, nA, γ = size(hw.R, 1), size(hw.R, 2), hw.γ decision = [s for s in 1:nS-1 if hw.T[s, 1, nS] < 1] # tiles that don't end the episode ε_greedy(q, ε, rng) = rand(rng) < ε ? rand(rng, 1:length(q)) : rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(q)), q)) # One learner = a function update!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′); N holds eligibility traces. q_learning!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (Q[s, a] += α * (r + γ * maximum(Q[s′, :]) - Q[s, a])) sarsa!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (Q[s, a] += α * (r + γ * Q[s′, a′] - Q[s, a])) function sarsa_λ!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1, λ = 0.5) N[s, a] += 1 δ = r + γ * Q[s′, a′] - Q[s, a] Q .+= α * δ .* N # every pair, in proportion to its trace N .*= γ * λ end function learn(update!, steps, rng; ε = 0.1) Q, N = zeros(nS, nA), zeros(nS, nA) s = rand(rng, decision) a = ε_greedy(Q[s, :], ε, rng) for t in 1:steps s′ = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(hw.T[s, a, :])) a′ = ε_greedy(Q[s′, :], ε, rng) update!(Q, N, s, a, hw.R[s, a], s′, a′) s, a = s′, a′ if s == nS # terminal: start a new episode s = rand(rng, decision) N .= 0.0 # traces don't cross episodes a = ε_greedy(Q[s, :], ε, rng) end end return Q end # True value of the greedy policy, by exact policy evaluation. function greedy_value(Q) π = [argmax(Q[s, :]) for s in 1:nS] Tπ = [hw.T[s, π[s], s′] for s in 1:nS, s′ in 1:nS] Rπ = [hw.R[s, π[s]] for s in 1:nS] return mean(((I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ)[decision]) end for (name, f) in (("Q-learning", q_learning!), ("Sarsa", sarsa!), ("Sarsa(λ)", sarsa_λ!)) v = mean(greedy_value(learn(f, 1000, MersenneTwister(seed))) for seed in 1:10) println(rpad(name, 12), "after 1,000 steps: ", round(v; digits = 2)) end @assert mean(greedy_value(learn(q_learning!, 30_000, MersenneTwister(seed))) for seed in 1:5) > 4.0 ``` ::: ### Function approximation and replay ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python class GradientQLearning: """Q-learning with a linear action value function Q_theta(s, a) = theta[a] @ features(s) (eq. 17.21), with the step's gradient scaled to norm at most 1. With replay > 0, experience tuples go into a buffer of that size and, every `every` steps, one step is taken along the average gradient of a random batch of `batch` tuples (eq. 17.22) instead. """ def __init__(self, features, n_features, n_actions, gamma, alpha, replay=0, batch=32, every=1): self.features, self.gamma, self.alpha = features, gamma, alpha self.theta = np.zeros((n_actions, n_features)) self.buffer = deque(maxlen=replay) if replay else None self.batch, self.every, self.t = batch, every, 0 def q(self, f): """Q values of all actions, for one feature vector f.""" return self.theta @ f def update(self, f, a, r, f2, done, rng): self.t += 1 if self.buffer is None: # One tuple: TD error times grad_theta Q = the features f. target = r + (0.0 if done else self.gamma * self.q(f2).max()) g = np.zeros_like(self.theta) g[a] = (target - self.q(f)[a]) * f else: self.buffer.append((f, a, r, f2, done)) if len(self.buffer) < self.batch or self.t % self.every: return pick = rng.integers(len(self.buffer), size=self.batch) F, A, R, F2, D = (np.array(x) for x in zip(*(self.buffer[i] for i in pick))) # Batched targets: (batch, n_actions) values of the next states. targets = R + np.where(D, 0.0, self.gamma * (F2 @ self.theta.T).max(1)) td = targets - (F * self.theta[A]).sum(axis=1) g = np.zeros_like(self.theta) np.add.at(g, A, td[:, None] * F) # sum rows per action g /= self.batch self.theta += self.alpha * scale_gradient(g, 1.0) def run_episode(learner, env_step, s0, rng, epsilon=0.0, max_steps=1000): """One episode of gradient Q-learning from state s0. env_step(s, a) returns (s2, r, done) for action index a. Actions are epsilon-greedy on the current Q. Returns the number of steps taken. """ s, f = s0, learner.features(s0) for t in range(1, max_steps + 1): a = epsilon_greedy(learner.q(f), epsilon, rng) s2, r, done = env_step(s, a) f2 = learner.features(s2) learner.update(f, a, r, f2, done, rng) if done: return t s, f = s2, f2 return max_steps ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra # Fourier features over (position, speed): cos/sin up to order 3 per axis, all products. lo, hi = [MOUNTAIN_CAR_X[1], MOUNTAIN_CAR_V[1]], [MOUNTAIN_CAR_X[2], MOUNTAIN_CAR_V[2]] function φ(s) z = (s .- lo) ./ (hi .- lo) # 0 to 1 across each axis axis(t) = [0.5; [sin(2π * i * t) for i in 1:3]; [cos(2π * i * t) for i in 1:3]] return vec(axis(z[1]) * axis(z[2])') # all pairwise products (outer product) end scaled(g) = norm(g) > 1 ? g ./ norm(g) : g # cap the step's length at 1 # One episode of gradient Q-learning; θ has one row of weights per action. # With a replay buffer, each step learns from a random batch of 32 stored tuples. function episode!(θ, rng; α = 0.3, buffer = nothing, cap = 1000) s = [-0.6 + 0.2rand(rng), 0.0] for t in 1:cap f = φ(s) q = θ * f a = rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(q)), q)) s′ = mountain_car_step(s, MOUNTAIN_CAR_ACTIONS[a]) done = mountain_car_goal(s′) batch = buffer === nothing ? [(f, a, φ(s′), done)] : (push!(buffer, (f, a, φ(s′), done)); length(buffer) < 32 ? [] : rand(rng, buffer, 32)) if !isempty(batch) g = zero(θ) for (fb, ab, f2, d) in batch # TD error × features, in action ab's row target = -1 + (d ? 0.0 : maximum(θ * f2)) g[ab, :] .+= (target - dot(θ[ab, :], fb)) .* fb end θ .+= α .* scaled(g ./ length(batch)) end done && return t s = s′ end return cap end nf = length(φ([0.0, 0.0])) for (name, buf) in (("gradient Q-learning", () -> nothing), ("with replay", () -> Any[])) late = mean(begin rng, θ, b = MersenneTwister(seed), zeros(3, nf), buf() lengths = [episode!(θ, rng; buffer = b) for _ in 1:60] mean(lengths[41:60]) end for seed in 1:3) println(rpad(name, 21), "steps per episode, episodes 41-60: ", round(late)) end ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reading the Julia code (for Python programmers)"} - **`q_learning!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (...)`** is a one-line function; keyword arguments come after the `;`. All three learners share one signature, so `learn` can take any of them. - **`Q .+= α * δ .* N`** updates the whole table in place, like `Q += alpha * delta * N` on NumPy arrays. - **`(I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ`** solves the linear system for the policy's values: `I` is the identity from `LinearAlgebra`, `\` is NumPy's `np.linalg.solve`. - **`vec(axis(z[1]) * axis(z[2])')`**: a column times a row (`'` transposes) gives the outer product, a 7 × 7 matrix of all products, flattened to 49 features. - **`(push!(...); expr)`** runs two expressions and returns the second, a compact way to append and then decide. - **`rand(rng, buffer, 32)`** draws 32 elements with replacement, like `rng.choice(len(buffer), 32)`. ::: ### Run them ::: {#a2ed8883 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} env = hex_world() learner = mf.QLearning(len(env.R), 6, env.gamma, alpha=0.1) terminal = len(env.R) - 1 decision = [s for s in range(terminal) if env.T[s, 0, terminal] < 1] mf.run_tabular(env, learner, 30_000, decision[0], np.random.default_rng(0), epsilon=0.1, reset=lambda s, rng: rng.choice(decision) if s == terminal else None) greedy_value = policy_evaluation_exact(env.T, env.R, env.gamma, learner.Q.argmax(axis=1))[decision].mean() ``` ::: ::: {#02aed123 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Q-learning on Hex World, 30,000 steps: greedy policy worth 4.41 (optimal 4.53) ``` ::: ::: ### Results #### Learning rates ::: {#cell-fig-incremental .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Incremental estimates of a mean wait of 8 minutes. Compute the incremental estimates with $\alpha = 0.25$, starting from $\hat x_0 = 20$. What weight does each sample have in the final estimate? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} $\hat x_1 = 20 + 0.25(20 - 20) = 20$; $\hat x_2 = 20 + 0.25(2) = 20.5$; $\hat x_3 = 20.5 + 0.25(-2.5) = 19.875$; $\hat x_4 = 19.875 + 0.25(4.125) \approx 20.91$. Sample $k$ steps before the last has weight $0.25 \times 0.75^k$: 0.25 for 24, 0.1875 for 18, 0.141 for 22, 0.105 for 20. The initial value keeps weight $0.75^4 \approx 0.32$. With a constant rate, the start is never fully forgotten, only exponentially discounted. ::: **Problem 2: one Q-learning step.** $\gamma = 0.9$, $\alpha = 0.2$. The agent takes $a$ in $s$, receives $r = 2$ and lands in $s'$ where $Q(s', \cdot) = (1, 4, 3)$. The current $Q(s, a) = 5$. What is the new $Q(s, a)$? What would Sarsa give if the next action were the third? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Q-learning: target $2 + 0.9 \times 4 = 5.6$, TD error $0.6$, new $Q(s, a) = 5 + 0.2 \times 0.6 = 5.12$. Sarsa with $a' = 3$: target $2 + 0.9 \times 3 = 4.7$, TD error $-0.3$, new $Q = 5 - 0.06 = 4.94$. The two updates even go in opposite directions, because Sarsa's target reflects the non-greedy action actually taken. ::: **Problem 3: shaping that loops.** A robot gets +1 when it reaches its charger. To help, a designer adds +0.5 every time the robot moves closer to the charger (by distance), and nothing for moving away. With $\gamma = 0.9$, why can this change the optimal policy? Fix it with a potential. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Moving away costs nothing, and moving back earns 0.5, so a two-step loop earns 0.5 every other step, worth about $0.5/(1 - 0.81) \approx 2.6$ discounted, forever. That beats reaching the charger for +1 once. Use $\beta(s) = -0.5 \times \text{distance}(s)$ and $F = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)$. Moving closer by one then earns about $+0.5$ and moving away costs about $-0.5$, so any loop nets roughly nothing (exactly a discount term), and the optimal policy is unchanged. ::: **Problem 4: how far back does a trace reach?** With $\gamma = 0.95$ and $\lambda = 0.9$, after how many steps does a pair's trace fall below 0.1 of its value when visited? What happens with $\lambda = 0$? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The trace decays by $\gamma\lambda = 0.855$ per step. $0.855^k < 0.1$ when $k > \ln 0.1 / \ln 0.855 \approx 14.7$, so after 15 steps. A reward found 15 steps after a decision still moves that decision's value by at least a tenth of the full amount. With $\lambda = 0$, traces vanish after one step: plain Sarsa, which updates only the most recent pair. ::: **Problem 5: why replay needs an off-policy learner.** The replay buffer holds transitions collected by older, worse policies. Why is that acceptable for Q-learning but not for Sarsa? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Q-learning's target, $r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')$, uses only $(s, a, r, s')$ and the current $Q$. It doesn't matter which policy chose $a$, because the target is about the greedy policy. Sarsa's target uses $a'$, the action the *behavior* policy took next. With old transitions, that is an old policy's action, so Sarsa would learn a mixture of outdated policies' values rather than the current one's. Replay pairs naturally with off-policy methods. ::: ## Recap 1. **Model-free learning is incremental averaging toward sampled targets (@eq-incremental).** *Why it matters:* the learning rate decides whether estimates converge (decaying) or track change (constant). That choice reappears in every method on this page and in deep reinforcement learning. 2. **Q-learning learns optimal values while exploring (@eq-q-learning).** *Why it matters:* it needs no model and converges to $Q^*$ under mild conditions. It is the ancestor of deep Q-networks. 3. **Sarsa learns the values of the policy it actually follows (@eq-sarsa).** *Why it matters:* when exploration is risky, on-policy learning is safer while training. On the towpath, Sarsa collected \-21 per episode against Q-learning's \-31, by choosing a longer, safer route. 4. **Eligibility traces and shaping speed up learning; only potential-based shaping is safe (@eq-traces, @eq-shaping).** *Why it matters:* sparse rewards are the norm in real problems. A careless bonus on the trail created a policy that never reaches the summit: reward hacking in miniature. 5. **Function approximation and experience replay scale Q-learning up (@eq-gradient-q, @eq-replay).** *Why it matters:* this pair, with a neural network in place of our linear features, is DQN. On the mountain car, replay cut the steps per episode from 178 to 123. ## Cheat sheet & connections | Name | Formula | Ref | |---|---|---| | Incremental mean | $\hat x \leftarrow \hat x + \alpha(x - \hat x)$; $\sum\alpha = \infty$, $\sum\alpha^2 < \infty$ | @eq-incremental | | ★ Q-learning | $Q(s, a) \mathrel{+}= \alpha(r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(s', a') - Q(s, a))$ | @eq-q-learning | | ★ Sarsa | $Q(s, a) \mathrel{+}= \alpha(r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a))$ | @eq-sarsa | | Sarsa(λ) | $Q \mathrel{+}= \alpha\delta N$, $N \leftarrow \gamma\lambda N$ | @eq-traces | | ★ Potential-based shaping | $F(s, a, s') = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)$ | @eq-shaping | | Gradient Q-learning | $\theta \mathrel{+}= \alpha(r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q_\theta(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a))\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s, a)$ | @eq-gradient-q | | Experience replay | average the gradient over a random batch from a buffer | @eq-replay | : Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name). {#tbl-cheatsheet} **Common pitfalls** - **A learning rate that decays too fast.** $\alpha = 1/m^{1.5}$ stops learning while the estimate is still wrong; constant rates never settle. - **Judging Q-learning by its training rewards.** It learns the greedy policy's values, but earns the exploring policy's rewards. Evaluate the greedy policy separately. - **Reward bonuses that can be farmed.** Any shaping reward that isn't a difference of potentials can create loops that pay more than the real goal. - **Eligibility traces with off-policy learning.** Cut the traces when an exploratory action is taken, or the greedy policy is credited with the explorer's luck. - **Divergence with function approximation.** Bootstrapping, off-policy learning and function approximation together can make the parameters blow up.
